Supreme Court defers AP municipal poll final list to October 25 on YSRCP plea, directs SEC to decide on nominations
The court holds that the YSRCP has made out a prima facie case in its plea for more time to file nominations

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) held that the
YSR Congress Party (YSRCP)
had made out a prima facie case in its plea for an extension of time to file nominations for the
urban local body elections
in
Andhra Pradesh
. The party had alleged that its candidates were
met with violence and blocked from filing nominations.
The court directed the State Election Commission (SEC) to postpone the publication of the final list of candidates till October 25.
Nominations end across 3 A.P. districts with no fresh violence after tense campaigning
The SEC was directed to consider the representations of the party and its candidates, including evidence and material as well as electronic evidence, and to take a decision on extending the last date for filing nominations in urban local bodies wherever it is of the view that candidates were unable to file. The decision is to be taken by Thursday (October 22).
Wherever the SEC chooses to extend the time, the extension shall not be less than 48 hours from the publication of the decision, which is to be done by amending the election notification.
Jagan alleges large-scale irregularities in local body poll nominations
The Director General of Police (DGP) was directed to take all necessary steps to provide security, maintain CCTV footage and file a compliance report in the Supreme Court.
The SEC was also directed to take the necessary decisions and issue orders to remove apprehensions from the minds of the petitioner and all concerned, and to file a compliance report. Nominations are also to be permitted at district headquarters.
Police fire six rounds in air to defuse tension in Pulivendula
The petition
The YSRCP, led by former Chief Minister Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy, had alleged that mass violence in the State prevented its candidates from filing nominations for the urban local body elections. It sought police protection for candidates, an extension of the deadline for filing nominations and the designation of additional and alternative nomination centres to enable candidates to submit their papers safely.

The plea, filed by party general secretary Lella Appireddy through advocate Mahfooz Ahsan Nazki, said several of its candidates were allegedly assaulted and physically prevented from reaching nomination centres during the nomination period, which began on October 16 and ended on October 18.
The High Court had dismissed the party’s application seeking an extension, holding that the deadline had expired and that extending it would amount to interference with the election process.

efet_body:
Delhi government directs officials to ensure timely disposal of public grievances
The directions follow a review by the chief secretary, who expressed concern over pendency of grievances
Updated on: Oct 21, 2026, 07:15:50 IST
By
Saloni Bhatia
Prefer HT
on Google

Copy link
Delhi Government Directs Timely Disposal of Grievances
The Delhi government, in a circular, directed officials to ensure time-bound disposal of public grievances, and warned that heads of departments will be held accountable for delays and poor-quality responses to complaints received through official redressal platforms.
A review of grievances will be conducted every Friday. (Representative file photo)
In the circular dated October 16, registrar of cooperative societies Krishna Kumar Singh issued instructions for monitoring complaints received through the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS), LG Listing, the Public Grievance Monitoring System (PGMS) and other grievance redressal platforms.
The directions follow a review by the chief secretary, who expressed concern over pendency of grievances and cases whose disposal had exceeded the prescribed timelines. The circular said necessary action would be taken against officials in departments where grievances were not disposed of on time.
Officials Asked to Monitor Pending Complaints
All branch and section in-charges have been asked to closely monitor complaints and ensure their disposal within the applicable timelines. Overdue grievances must be taken up on priority, while officials have been directed to regularly track pending cases and take timely action to prevent further delays, as per the circular.
Also Read:
NTA issues grievance advisory: Application number, registered email mandatory
Clear Responses and Rules for Transferring Complaints
The order also emphasises the quality of grievance disposal, stating that merely submitting a reply cannot be considered satisfactory. “Each complaint must be examined on its merits, with officials required to provide clear, specific and reasoned responses and ensure that necessary action has been taken,” the order read.
Further, complaints cannot be transferred to another department or authority without prior approval from the head of the department, the circular stated, adding that any proposal for transfer must clearly state the reasons and establish the jurisdiction of the authority to which the grievance is being referred.
Weekly Reviews and Accountability
A review of grievances will be conducted every Friday, covering pending and overdue cases, overall pendency and the quality of disposal. Branch and section in-charges must also compile consolidated data on complaints received, disposed of, pending and overdue across the various platforms. The data must include age-wise pendency and the action taken in each case.
Also Read:
Ludhiana MC’s building branch tops pending grievances list: PGRS report
The circular further directs officials to prioritise grievances pending under the CM Jansunwai programme, along with old and unresolved complaints.
It also cautions officials against mechanically closing complaints or disposing them without an appropriate and satisfactory response. Branch and section in-charges will be responsible for ensuring compliance and monitoring the performance of officials dealing with grievances. Avoidable delays, repeated pendency and deficiencies in disposal quality will be viewed seriously, the circular said.

CJP’s Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka withdraw Delhi High Court plea against extension of judicial custody
The CJP co-convenors will decide on their further course of action after another hearing before the Special Executive Magistrate court today
Updated

Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were taken into custody on October 13 after they climbed over a locked gate to enter Jantar Mantar following its de-notification as a protest site. Credit: X/@Cockroachisback
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) withdrew their petitions in the Delhi High Court challenging their judicial custody by a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM). This comes after the High Court agreed to urgently hear the matter.
The CJP co-convenors will decide on their further course of action after another hearing before the Special Executive Magistrate court on Wednesday (October 21, 2026).
Mr. Das and Mr. Ranka had earlier assailed the SEM's October 19 order remanding them to two days' judicial custody in the High Court, which is shut this week due to Dussehra vacation.
Delhi Police transfers two cases against CJP’s Das, Ranka to Crime Branch
While permitting the two to withdraw the case, the judge clarified that he has not made observations on the merit of the matter.
During the hearing, the court orally observed that a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution was not an appropriate remedy in this case.
Mr. Das and Mr. Ranka were taken into custody on October 13 after they allegedly climbed over a locked gate to enter Jantar Mantar, which had earlier been denotified as a designated protest site, and were sent to five-day judicial custody. A newly-appointed Special Executive Magistrate at Mandir Marg police station on Monday (October 19, 2026) ordered their judicial remand till October 21 after they were produced before him.
ALSO WATCH
CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka’s judicial custody extended by two days
Along with other CJP workers, Mr. Das and Mr. Ranka displayed the national flag at the site and shouted slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar before being detained and placed under preventive arrest on October 13.
The two were first sent to judicial custody for five days on October 14 by a Special Executive Magistrate. According to Delhi Police, the protesters allegedly entered the denotified protest site by trespassing through private premises and obstructed police personnel from discharging their official duties.
The CJP has alleged that the bail proceedings in the case have been deliberately delayed to prevent the release of its two co-convenors.
Neha Bora moves Delhi High Court against peace bond notice
Justice Subramonium Prasad will also take up a separate petition by the All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora against a Delhi Police's October 17 notice asking for the execution of a bond before a SEM for "keeping peace".
Neha Bora's plea pertains to a notice dated October 17 under section 126 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), asking the student leader to appear before the SEM on October 19 and show cause on why there should not be execution of a personal bond of ₹10,000 with one surety "for keeping peace for a period of enquiry". The AISA President was taken into preventive detention on October 16 and released on October 17 after a group was stopped from participating in the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)'s '
Lehra Do Tiranga
' march.

FSSAI’s new pesticide residue limits for tea: What consumers and industry need to know
FSSAI has proposed maximum residue limits (MRLs) of 20 ppm for acetamiprid and 50 ppm for imidacloprid in tea, with the draft regulations open for stakeholder consultation
Timsy Jaipuria
18 Oct 2026 3:45 PM IST
Click the Play button to hear this message in audio format
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed new maximum residue limits (MRLs) for two pesticides – acetamiprid and imidacloprid – in tea, marking another step in the country's ongoing review of food safety standards. The proposed limits are intended to provide clearer regulatory benchmarks for pesticide residues and strengthen monitoring across the tea supply chain.
Under the draft Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette of India on October 16, FSSAI has proposed an MRL of 20 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg), or parts per million (ppm), for acetamiprid and 50 mg/kg for imidacloprid in tea. The draft regulations are open to stakeholder consultation and are subject to finalisation.
For consumers, the key distinction is that these are proposed regulatory limits, not finalised standards. An MRL specifies the maximum legally permitted pesticide residue concentration in a food commodity. It does not, by itself, indicate the amount of pesticide a person consumes in a cup of tea or establish the health risk from a particular residue level.
How India's proposed limits compare internationally
The proposed acetamiprid limit of 20 ppm is lower than the corresponding limits of 30 ppm in Japan and 50 ppm in the United States, according to the information accompanying the proposal. The proposed imidacloprid limit has been framed with reference to international Codex standards.
Also Read:
FSSAI proposes ban on sucrose, fructose in foods for babies up to 6 months: What parents need to know
Such comparisons provide context for India's regulatory approach, but they should be interpreted carefully. Different countries may set residue limits based on crop-specific agricultural practices, authorised pesticide uses, residue studies and regulatory assessments. A lower MRL does not automatically mean that a country's tea is safer, just as a higher limit does not necessarily mean that a product poses a health risk.
The significance of the proposed Indian standards will depend on the scientific evidence underpinning them, the applicable enforcement framework and the final regulations notified by the food safety authority.
What does this mean for tea drinkers?
For households, tea remains a widely consumed everyday product, making effective residue monitoring an important part of food safety oversight. Clearly defined limits can help food businesses and enforcement agencies assess compliance and identify products that do not meet prescribed standards.
Also Read:
FSSAI orders Everest to recall cumin powder from market after sample found ‘unsafe’
However, consumers should not interpret the proposal as evidence that tea currently available in the market is unsafe. Nor does the announcement establish that all tea products contain either pesticide. Actual residue levels vary depending on cultivation practices, pesticide application, processing and other factors.
Consumers can continue to make informed purchasing decisions by choosing products from reputable manufacturers, checking packaging and following official food safety advisories. The draft proposal does not, on its own, warrant a change in normal tea-drinking habits.
Implications for growers and the tea industry
For tea growers, processors, exporters and testing laboratories, the proposed limits could provide greater clarity on compliance requirements once the rules are finalised. The industry may need to assess pesticide-use practices, testing protocols and supply-chain controls against the eventual standards.
Pesticides play a role in managing crop pests and limiting agricultural losses. Parents buying infant nutrition products may see tighter safeguards on added sugars if a proposed food safety amendment takes effect, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) seeking to prohibit the addition of sucrose and fructose in products intended for babies up to six months of age.
The food regulator has published a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, in the Gazette of India on October 16. The proposal would prohibit manufacturers from adding sucrose and fructose to infant nutrition products meant for this age group, strengthening existing rules that allow these sugars under specified conditions.
For consumers, the move could mean stricter controls over how infant nutrition products are formulated, with a greater emphasis on age-appropriate carbohydrate sources. However, the proposal is still at the draft stage and is not yet a final regulatory requirement.
What changes for parents?
Under the existing regulations, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred carbohydrate sources in infant nutrition products. Sucrose and fructose may currently be added when needed as a carbohydrate source, subject to a combined limit of 20 per cent of total carbohydrates.

The proposed amendment would remove this allowance for products intended for infants up to six months of age. If finalised, manufacturers would have to reformulate products in this category to comply with the new restriction.
For parents, the key takeaway is that the proposed change concerns the ingredients manufacturers may add to infant nutrition products. It does not mean that all carbohydrates will be prohibited, nor does it establish that every product currently on the market contains added sucrose or fructose.
Why does it matter for infant health?
The first six months are a critical period for infant growth and development, when feeding choices and nutritional adequacy are particularly important. Reducing the scope for adding sucrose and fructose to products for this age group is intended to strengthen safeguards against unnecessary exposure to these sugars.
The broader public health concern is that early dietary exposure to added sugars can contribute to the development of taste preferences for sweet foods and may form part of dietary patterns associated with future health risks. However, the proposed amendment itself does not establish that removing these ingredients will, on its own, prevent childhood obesity or other health conditions.

The immediate impact on consumers is uncertain. If the amendment is finalised, manufacturers may need to review ingredient sourcing, formulations, production processes and product labelling to ensure compliance.
Whether these changes affect retail prices, product availability or the range of formulations offered will depend on how manufacturers respond and how the final rules are framed. The draft notification does not announce a price change, a product recall or an immediate withdrawal of existing products.
Parents should therefore not assume that products currently available are automatically unsafe or that they need to switch products in anticipation of the proposal. Any feeding changes for young infants should be made with appropriate medical advice.

The regulator found cattle-feed bran being used in biscuit manufacturing, detergent/caustic soda in a Dodla Dairy milk sample and pesticide residues in yellow raisins sold by UEIR Organic Foods.
In a social media post on Saturday, FSSAI said it had "initiated legal proceedings for prosecution" against the three companies over "serious food safety violations".
The action against Surya Food & Agro, which manufactures Priyagold biscuits, follows an inspection conducted by FSSAI after a consumer complaint.
The inspection revealed serious food safety and hygiene deficiencies, including the use of cattle-feed bran as a raw material in biscuit manufacturing.

FSSAI also found deficiencies in plant hygiene, pest control, raw material storage and segregation, personnel hygiene, premises maintenance and the handling of intermediate formulations.

A regulatory sample of 'Full Cream Milk' was collected from the company and sent for analysis.
The Food Analyst declared it substandard due to non-conformity with the prescribed milk fat requirements.
Following an appeal by the company, the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory, which "confirmed that the sample was unsafe due to the presence of detergent/caustic soda and substandard due to milk fat below the minimum prescribed limit."
The laboratory findings established violations relating to unsafe and substandard food under the Food Safety and Standards Act (FSS Act), 2006.
The competent authority granted sanction for initiating prosecution against Dodla Dairy and the other concerned food business operators (FBOs) associated with the manufacture and marketing of the product.
The authorities also directed further prosecution proceedings in connection with the unsafe and substandard food.

FSSAI's action against UEIR Organic Foods follows the detection of pesticide residues in a sample of yellow raisins sold by the company.
The regulator initiated legal proceedings for prosecution against the company as part of its action against serious food safety violations.

Food regulator flags hygiene violations at Radisson Blu, misleading claims for rice bran oil on e-commerce platforms, and suspends or cancels licences of two food businesses

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has taken action against a hotel, three food businesses and two e-commerce platforms for food safety non-compliance and misleading claims, the regulator said in social media posts on Friday.
The action covers AB Hotels Limited (Radisson Blu Hotel), DNV Food Products Limited, Jhanvitanni, Gemini Edibles and Fats India Limited, and e-commerce platforms BigBasket and Flipkart India.
The regulator further issued an improvement notice to Radisson Blu Hotel over poor maintenance of premises and equipment, such as rusted machinery, freezer leakage and deficiencies in refrigeration, temperature monitoring, ventilation, flooring and lighting.
“Inadequate cleaning and sanitisation, stagnant water, drainage and food-waste issues, and deficiencies in pest control were observed, including cockroach and fly activity,” it said. “Food procurement and receiving checks were inadequate, including receipt of fungal-affected and deteriorated fruits and vegetables, with deficiencies in approved-vendor records and traceability.”
Cooking oil suitability checks were not carried out as required, and oils with TPC (total polar compounds) values of 31 and 24.4 were found in use in the NYC Kitchen, said the regulator. There was improper segregation of raw and cooked foods, vegetarian and non-vegetarian items, allergenic and non-allergenic foods, and food and non-food items. Food handlers were found working without gloves and hairnets, wearing jewellery and with long nails.

The FBO (food business operator) has been directed to take immediate corrective measures and submit a detailed action taken report (ATR), with supporting documentary and photographic evidence. Failure to comply may lead to the suspension of the FSSAI licence, according to the regulator.
FSSAI also issued a notice to Gemini Edibles and Fats India Limited, Innovative Retail Concepts Private Limited (BigBasket) and Flipkart India over misleading claims for “Freedom Cooking Rice Bran Oil.”
According to the regulator, the product was promoted on e-commerce platforms and social media with claims such as “Reduces bad cholesterol and maintains/increases good cholesterol” and “10,000+ PPM Natural Oryzanol,” linking its consumption to cholesterol management and heart health.
FSSAI found that these claims are not covered or permitted for edible vegetable oil (rice bran oil) under the Advertising and Claims Regulations, 2018. It also noted that Gemini Edibles and Fats India Limited was offering food products through its own e-commerce website without appearing to hold a valid central licence covering e-commerce activity.
The FBOs have been directed to show cause why action should not be initiated under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the rules and regulations made under it.
DNV Food Products Limited had its licence suspended after FSSAI said it had observed food being manufactured and stored amid inadequate cleaning, stagnant water, cobwebs and flies, including a fly in direct contact with papad. Food handlers were found not wearing gloves and masks. Processing equipment was rusted, while flooring was damaged, walls were damp, paint was flaking, and ventilation and lighting were inadequate.
Products were processed and repacked without the required licence endorsement, and food-grade packaging certificates, migration reports and mock recall records were unavailable, according to the regulator.
FSSAI also cancelled the licence of Jhanvitanni after continued non-compliance with food safety requirements and operation despite licence suspension, it said. Severe hygiene and sanitation deficiencies were observed at the premises.
Corrective actions submitted by the FBO were found unsatisfactory, said FSSAI, with several previously identified non-compliances remaining unaddressed. Maharashtra FDA bans loose spice powder sales, orders Statewide crackdown on adulteration
The Food Safety Commissioner’s order bans prohibited colouring agents, including Metanil Yellow and Rhodamine B, and adulterants such as brick powder and chalk, and requires all spice powders to be packed and sealed at the place of production before sale
Updated

Yohaan Varghese
READ LATER
SEE ALL
Remove
Manufacturers have been directed to maintain clean, dry and pest-free premises, with drying spices on public roads, near drains, garbage bins or cattle sheds strictly prohibited. Image for the purpose of representation only.
| Photo Credit: File
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has prohibited the sale of loose, unpackaged spice powders and mixed spices across the State as part of a crackdown on adulteration, unhygienic manufacturing practices and misleading labelling. The order, issued by Food Safety Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe on Thursday (October 15, 2026) mandates stricter safety standards across the spice supply chain, from manufacturing to retail sale.
The directive covers manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers, e-commerce operators, hotels, restaurants and caterers dealing in spices, including turmeric, chilli, coriander, cumin, black pepper and mixed spice products. All spice powders and mixed spices must be packed and sealed at the place of production before distribution or sale.
The FDA has banned the use of prohibited colouring agents, including Metanil Yellow, Rhodamine B, Sudan dyes and Lead Chromate, along with adulterants such as brick powder, chalk, sawdust, and foreign starch. The sale of inferior-quality spices and spices from which extracts have been removed is also prohibited.
The order further prohibits the use of ethylene oxide for sterilising spices, citing its potential carcinogenic effects. Spices will be tested for pesticide residues, aflatoxins, heavy metals, and other contaminants.
Manufacturers have been directed to maintain clean, dry and pest-free premises, with drying spices on public roads, near drains, garbage bins or cattle sheds strictly prohibited. All operators must possess valid FSSAI licences or registrations, as a trade licence alone will not authorise spice manufacturing or grinding.
Packaged spices must carry mandatory information, including ingredients, manufacturer details, FSSAI licence number, batch number and manufacturing and expiry dates. Unsubstantiated claims regarding purity, organic production or health benefits will attract action.
Action to extend beyond retailers
In cases of adulteration, the FDA will trace the source of contamination and investigate manufacturers, grinding units, repackaging businesses and suppliers of prohibited substances, rather than restricting action to retailers.
Officials will examine purchase records, production details and batch numbers to identify violations. Depending on their severity, action may include seizure of products, market recalls, suspension or cancellation of licences and prosecution.
Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, selling substandard food can attract fines of up to ₹5 lakh, while misleading advertisements can result in penalties of up to ₹10 lakh. Cases where unsafe food causes death can attract imprisonment ranging from seven years to life, along with a minimum fine of ₹10 lakh.
The FDA has directed food safety officers across Maharashtra to conduct compliance inspections and submit monthly enforcement reports. Designated Officers must report to Divisional Joint Commissioners by the third of every month, while consolidated reports must reach the Commissioner’s office by the fifth.
Consumers can report suspected adulteration, unhygienic production or misleading labelling through the FDA’s toll-free helpline, 1800 222 365, or its online grievance portal at complaints.mahafda.in.

A peon’s 11-year wait for pension has shaken up Uttar Pradesh’s bureaucracy and judiciary, with the

It was only after Jagdish Prasad Tripathi, who retired as a peon in 2016 after 32 years of service approached the Supreme Court that the extent of the delay came to light. (ANI)
A bench of justices KV Viswanathan and Arun Palli, which also asked the

What happened to Tripathi, the bench said, was an “unfortunate calamity” that should not befall any other employee. It directed the chief secretary to submit by December 31 a report explaining why his pension papers were not cleared immediately after retirement, identifying the officials responsible for the delay, detailing proposed action against them, and explaining how the state proposed to compensate him for the “serious violation” of his rights and “grave injustice”.
The court also directed the chief secretary to issue necessary orders or standard operating procedures, if not already in place, to ensure that pension papers of employees legitimately entitled to their dues are not delayed.

The matter was not listed thereafter. Even an application filed by Tripathi in October 2025 seeking early disposal was eventually disposed of in April 2026 without fixing a date for hearing.
It was only after Tripathi approached the Supreme Court that the extent of the delay came to light.
Reading through the records, the bench said it was “shocked” to find that for nearly a decade after his superannuation, “for no fault of the petitioner”, he had not been paid his retiral dues. Sankaranarayanan informed the court about a curative plea filed by one of the petitioners, which may be decided on its own merits. He pointed out that the present plea is an application seeking recall.
The application seeks recall on the ground that Justice Sharma ought to have recused as his son appears for the Election Commission of India (ECI) before the Madhya Pradesh high court.

On September 23, a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma gave a split verdict on whether the 2023 law should be referred to a Constitution bench. While Justice Datta was of the view that the need does not arise as the challenge to the Act can be considered based on the settled principles laid down by earlier judgments, Justice Sharma held a different view. He said that substantial questions on the interpretation of the Constitution arise in the matter and under Article 145(3), the same should be heard by a bench of at least five judges of the Supreme Court. The two judges passed a common order placing the matter before CJI for referring the petitions to a Constitution bench.
The plea seeks recall only of Justice Sharma’s order and the common order passed by the bench referring the matter to a Constitution Bench.

The application categorically states that the matter was heard by the bench of Justices Datta and Sharma on five occasions. On none of the occasions, Justice Sharma disclosed this fact or sought recusal on this ground. Sherstra stated that the fact about Justice Sharma’s son being engaged as ECI counsel became known from news reports that surfaced two days after the September 23 order.
It sought recall of the order stating, “The question is whether the established circumstances, viewed objectively, give rise to a reasonable apprehension concerning impartiality.” However, the application does not seek recall of Justice Datta’s separate opinion.
The application states the batch of petitions against the 2023 law was heard by the bench of Justices Datta and Sharma on five occasions – May 6, May 7, May 14, May 27 and July 30. It was on July 30 that orders were reserved on the issue of whether the petitions should be heard by a Constitution bench of five judges. However, not on a single occasion did the judge convey his possible conflict of interest and seek recusal.
If this fact was earlier known to them, they would have requested Justice Sharma’s recusal, the plea stated, while adding, “The absence of disclosure deprived the petitioners of an opportunity to raise that request before the opinions and order dated September 23 were pronounced.”

You pick up an apple, peel off the little sticker, give it a good wash and take a bite. Seems perfectly fine, right?
Well, there’s one extra step India’s food safety regulator wants you to follow.
The
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
(FSSAI) has advised consumers not to simply remove stickers from fruits and vegetables and wash the produce. Instead, it says the skin or the portion where the sticker was placed should be peeled or cut away before eating.
The reason? The adhesive used to stick those tiny labels to the produce can leave residue behind.
So, what should you actually do?
It's pretty simple.
If there's a sticker on your apple, orange, avocado or any other fruit, remove it first.
Then peel the skin or cut away the small patch where the sticker was attached.
You don't need to throw away the fruit. And there's no need to panic if you've already eaten a stickered fruit after simply washing it.
The advice is essentially about taking an extra precaution and avoiding direct consumption of any residue that may be left behind.
Why are fruits covered in stickers anyway?
Those little labels are something most of us barely notice, especially when doing our weekly grocery shopping.
But they're there for a reason. Fruit stickers can carry codes used by retailers to identify the produce and its price. Depending on the product and retailer, they may also provide other information about the fruit.
What they aren't, however, is edible packaging.
So even if the sticker comes off easily, it's better not to assume that the surface underneath is completely free of adhesive.
Is washing the fruit not enough?
Washing your fruits and vegetables is still important. But in the case of produce that has had a sticker stuck directly onto its skin, FSSAI's advice is to go one step further.
Remove the sticker and then peel or cut away the area where it was stuck.
For something like an apple, that's easy enough. If you're eating the fruit without peeling it, simply cutting off that small patch is another option.
Why the sticker maybe harmful?
Don't panic.
If you've ever discovered halfway through eating an apple that the tiny sticker has somehow vanished, you're certainly not alone
Do you need to throw the fruit away?
No.
A sticker doesn't mean the entire fruit is unsafe. Once you've removed the label, simply peel or cut off the area where it was attached.
And yes, you should still wash the fruit properly before eating it and that's because the glue in the sticker maybe harmful for your health.
The next time you're about to bite into that supermarket apple, take a second look at the sticker. Peel it off, remove the small stickered patch and then eat the fruit.
It's a tiny extra step. But when it comes to something you eat, it doesn't hurt to be a little careful.
